drills.title: Mask a card number before logging
drills.prompt: Arrange the lines so the program hides all but the last four digits of the card number. Two lines do not belong.
drills.explain: re.sub(pattern, replacement, text) takes the pattern first, then what to put in, then the text to search. The \1 in the replacement stands for the first group, the last four digits, so only they survive. Write patterns as raw strings (r"..."): in a normal string \b is a backspace character, not a word boundary, so the pattern silently stops matching.

drills.title: Validate a PIN code
drills.prompt: Fill the three blanks so a PIN code is valid only when the whole text is 6 digits and does not start with 0.
code: ok = re.___(r"___\d{___}", pin) is not None
drills.explain: Validation means the whole string must fit the pattern, so use re.fullmatch. re.match only anchors at the start (5600011 would pass because its first 6 characters fit) and re.search finds a match anywhere. [1-9] is the first digit without 0, so 060001 is refused, and then exactly 5 more digits follow: \d{5}. With {6} no 6-character PIN could ever pass.

drills.title: Do type hints stop anything?
drills.prompt: Read the code and type exactly what it prints, one line per line of output.
drills.explain: Type hints are notes for people and tools such as mypy or the editor. Python does not check them when the program runs. average((4, 6)) works because sum() and len() accept a tuple even though the hint says list, and the variable hinted as int simply holds the text "ten". A type checker would flag both lines, but running the file does not.

drills.title: The order id that was not found
drills.prompt: The ID is clearly in the text, yet the program crashes with an AttributeError. Click the line that causes it, then choose the right fix.
drills.explain: re.match only tries to match at the very start of the text, which begins with Order, so it returns None, and None has no .group(). re.search looks for the pattern anywhere. re.fullmatch needs the whole text to fit, and re.findall returns a list of strings, which has no .group() either. Whenever a regex function can return None, check it before calling .group().

drills.title: Review the AI's text-cleaning helpers
drills.prompt: An AI assistant wrote these helpers for an invoice dump. They run on the sample calls, but tick the statements that point at real problems.

issues.text: extract_amount crashes with AttributeError when the text has no amount, although the hint promises a float
issues.why: re.search returns None when nothing matches, and None has no .group(). Check the result first and decide what to return or raise (for example a ValueError with a clear message).

issues.text: The pattern in mask_card is a normal string, not a raw string
issues.why: It only works because \d happens to be left alone by Python (newer versions warn about it). A pattern such as \b would turn into a backspace character. Always write patterns as r"...".

issues.text: clean keeps "7x" although it is not made only of digits
issues.why: re.match only anchors at the start, so "7x" passes because it begins with a digit. For "all digits" use re.fullmatch(r"\d+", x) or x.isdigit().

issues.text: Names like s, t, x and tmp say nothing, and mask_card has no type hints
issues.why: Clear names (text, items, digits_only) and hints such as text: str make the code readable for people, editors and AI assistants.

non_issues.text: -> float is wrong because group(1) is text
non_issues.why: float() converts the text to a number, so the function really returns a float.

non_issues.text: "\\1" in the replacement is a typo and should be "\1"
non_issues.why: In a normal string "\\1" is a backslash followed by 1, which is what re.sub reads as group 1. A single "\1" would be the character with code 1.

non_issues.text: mask_card will raise an error because it has no type hints
non_issues.why: Type hints are optional and never checked at run time. Adding them is good style, not a requirement.

drills.explain: For regex code, ask what happens when nothing matches (None), whether the function anchors the way the name promises (match vs fullmatch), and whether patterns are raw strings. For clean code, ask whether a stranger could tell from the names and hints what goes in and out.
